Kentucky heritage behind globally familiar spirits and wines, with a growing international network of restaurants, hotels and listening clubs.
James Hatfield founded the distillery in Bardstown, Kentucky, in 1952. Today, master distiller Carolyn Hatfield-Moore oversees the whiskey’s production, quality and maturation.

Hatfield Group belongs to Walker Holdings, with heritage protections preserving the Hatfield name and production standards. Everyday spirits and regional wines reach ordinary shops alongside premium and allocated releases. The hospitality network has 306 operating venues: 240 Bar & Grills, 52 Inns, 12 Stave clubs and two Still Houses, with further signed projects kept separate from the open count.

At Albury, Hatfield’s full commercial spirits and wine families are within the house selection alongside bottles from other producers. Original, Small Batch, Rye, Wheated Bourbon, Bottled in Bond, Single Barrel, longer-aged and allocated bourbon expressions, Hatfield gin, and estate, premium and regional wines can be drawn on; Crispin or Harjit confirms actual cellar stock. The private Alex family barrel is not a bar listing. Hatfield Original also goes into the kitchen’s bourbon–black cherry confiture.

What guests keep & how the welcome works

This file owns the use and ownership of Albury's marked household goods, overnight welcome provision, stationery packs and selected guest gifts at the 11 August 2025 opening. It supersedes fixed departure tiers and older image captions that imply every dinner guest receives an identical bag.

Provision is generous, discreet and adapted to the guest. These are opening capabilities and ordinary service arrangements, not new booked visits, an account of gifts already accepted, or a retail launch. A guest can receive a fresh example of an otherwise household object as a gift. Staff make that clear naturally and use gift stock; they do not strip used room equipment into a departure bag or turn a casual visit into an inventory explanation.

The house holds fresh gift stock of the marked travel coffee cup, reusable water bottle, ceramic mug, boxed house-scent candle, coaster set, larger notebook/stationery set and waffle dressing gown. Cup and bottle may be offered individually or together in a fitted presentation box. A fresh flannel can accompany a bath gift; the flannel in the older departure photograph is a gift example, not permission to remove working linen.

These are thoughtful choices, not a compulsory bundle for every visitor. A friend who admires the mug may be given a new one; someone heading to the airport may appreciate a travel cup or bottle; a regular guest may keep a robe at Albury or take a fresh gifted one. A return visit need not produce a second folio, bottle or robe. Staff know the context or ask one ordinary question.
The take-home pack is a compact bookcloth presentation folio containing:
One A5 clothbound notebook and one pocket notebook.
One metal pen and one graphite pencil.
Ten sheets of ivory writing paper and ten matching envelopes.
Four correspondence cards and two Albury street-elevation postcards.

The folio, notebook covers and custom paper goods carry the architectural house mark. The whole pack is the guest's. It is distinct from the permanent leather correspondence folder in the bedroom. A small 'Yours to keep' card can make ownership clear. Wi-Fi, contact extensions and service information are supplied separately on the room-information card; no invented password, phone number or service timetable is fixed here.

Before an overnight arrival, a reusable lidded wicker basket is placed on the guest-room console. It has a washable Albury-marked linen lining and a restrained leather handle/strap treatment. It is a room welcome basket, distinct from the picnic hamper and from a gifted food basket.

The food, waters and stationery are for the guest; the basket remains with the room. A couple shares one sensibly sized basket with sufficient food and drink; personal stationery and travel items follow the actual guests. Replenishment follows use, not a daily ceremonial replacement of the entire hamper. Returning friends receive familiar favourites and fresh consumables without automatic duplicate keepsakes.

Robes, slippers, bathroom supplies and bedside water are already in their normal places. A chosen travel cup or reusable bottle is an additional personal gift, not compulsory in every arrival basket. House cordial and any other preparation requiring chilling wait in the guest refrigerator or are served chilled; the welcome note can mention them. A soft drink may be provided to the guest’s own preference alongside the standard waters. No wine or alcohol is assumed for every guest.

A separate food gift is assembled for the guest and journey, using a marked gift basket or suitable carrier. This basket and the packed contents belong to the recipient; it is not the room basket removed from stock.

The illustrated six-item example contains Seville marmalade (P01), bourbon and black cherry confiture (P05, with Hatfield Original credited), house mustard (P09), seeded rye crackers (P19), butter shortbread (P21), and rosemary/smoked-salt almonds (P23). It is an example of the available repertoire, not a mandatory six-product formula. Ketchup, other preserves, biscuits, snacks or cordial can be chosen. Chilled goods need a suitable journey and cold provision; nothing becomes shelf-stable because it is wrapped as a gift. Individual gifts use appropriate contents, batch/date, storage and allergen information.

Dinner guests may leave with a small food gift, a useful house object or nothing formal. The old 'Tier Two' photograph remains an optional assortment of available items; the mandatory fixed ten-item departure rule is retired. Staying guests can have their personal provisions and remaining treats packed for them. No guest must perform gratitude or attend a gift presentation for the scene to move on.

Ottilie oversees the welcome standard. Housekeeping prepares the room and basket; Crispin and the service team coordinate guest preferences, drinks and departure packing; Rafael and Bethan supply the food. Existing staff and stores handle this work; no new posts or employment arrangements are created. Gifts are household hospitality unless later play establishes a separate commercial arrangement.

Full-colour and white-led versions use the same inventories. Full colour uses bottle green, oxblood, dusty blue and warm ochre with ivory and muted gold. White-led custom surfaces are mostly warm ivory with narrow coloured trims and the same mark. Wicker remains natural and glass remains glass. Pantry jars retain Rafael's charcoal-and-gold labels in both versions; house syrups and cordials use the short clear, gold-capped bottle and ivory/bottle-green ALBURY label, without a chef name or architectural mark on the front. Colour is not a price tier or a ranking of guests.

Limestone Springs waters retain their producer identity. The still-water reference has an LS crest, blue label and pale limestone band; the sparkling-water reference has its fountain emblem and blue label. Albury does not replace either with house branding. Source catalogue:

The permanent never-sell ban remains retired. At opening no shop, public prices, retail orders or launch are established. Ordinary private gifts do not imply paid social posting, public access to Albury or involvement by Rosie and Homer in its management.

Limestone Springs was founded in Frankfort, Kentucky, in 2002. Its full beverage range launched in 2015, building a business in waters, sodas and mixers around Kentucky limestone-filtered water.

Part of Hatfield Group within Walker Holdings, Limestone Springs is an established global brand sold in more than ninety countries. Selected waters, mixers and sodas are routinely found in supermarkets, convenience stores, independent neighbourhood shops, hotels, restaurants, cocktail bars and airports.

At Albury, house still and sparkling water, Soda/Club Soda, mixers and bottled soft drinks are Limestone Springs. The available range supports the occasion and the actual order. The producer’s own labels remain part of table and bar service.

Kentucky-source still and sparkling water is bottled at source. Mixers and sodas also use audited regional manufacturing to Limestone specifications, with actual production origin stated on pack. Properly brewed Cream Soda retains its brewing process.
